reconcile.connective: JFB reads John 12:27 as a genuine petition paralleling Gethsemane's -- the plea and its resolution, submission to the Father's will, given together in the same verse.

discrepancy.connective: Louis Ruprecht argues John rewrote the Gethsemane prayer itself: his Jesus does not ask to be spared but pointedly declines even to voice the request.

skeptic.name: Louis A. Ruprecht Jr.
skeptic.work: This Tragic Gospel: How John Corrupted the Heart of Christianity
skeptic.attribution: Louis A. Ruprecht Jr., This Tragic Gospel: How John Corrupted the Heart of Christianity (Jossey-Bass, 2008)

excerpts.excerpt_text: To take this as a question--"Shall I say, Father, save me," &c.--as some eminent editors and interpreters do, is unnatural and jejune. It is a real petition, like that in Gethsemane, "Let this cup pass from Me"; only whereas there He prefaces the prayer with an "If it be possible," here He follows it up with what is tantamount to that--"Nevertheless for this cause came I unto this hour." The sentiment conveyed, then, by the prayer, in both cases, is twofold: (1) that only one thing could reconcile Him to the death of the cross--its being His Father's will He should endure it--and (2) that in this view of it He yielded Himself freely to it.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB explicitly rejects reading v. 27 as a merely rhetorical question and instead equates it with the Gethsemane petition, arguing both express the identical twofold sentiment (a real plea, instantly resolved into free submission) -- the most direct harmonization of the two prayers in the gathered notes.

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871), note on John 12:27
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats John 12:27 directly as a real petition structurally parallel to the Gethsemane prayer, arguing both convey the same twofold sentiment -- reluctance overcome by submission to the Father's will. (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies was checked via full-text search of the 1874 edition for 'Gethsemane,' 'cup pass,' and John 12:27/xii.27 and has no entry treating this pairing, so this row-surfaced harmonizing commentary is used per the spec's fallback.)
